Every "how does a database work" explanation is better after you have written one. This project builds a log-structured merge store in ~800 lines: durable writes, a sorted in-memory table, immutable on-disk tables, and compaction.

What it is: tiny-db — put(k, v), get(k), delete(k), scan(range), with a write-ahead log so a crash never loses an acknowledged write.

What you learn

Skill Where it comes from
Binary formats length-prefixed records, checksums, endianness
Crash safety WAL, fsync ordering, atomic rename
Data structures BTreeMap memtable, sorted SSTables, bloom filters
I/O performance buffered writers, mmap, sequential reads
Testing invariants property tests over a model implementation

Milestones

# Ship Done when
1 In-memory map put/get work
2 WAL replay after a kill -9 loses nothing
3 Flush to SSTable memory stays bounded at 10k keys
4 Read path memtable → newest SSTable → oldest
5 Compaction 20 SSTables merge into one
6 Correctness proof proptest against BTreeMap

The write path

Gotcha: flush() only drains the userspace buffer. sync_data() is what survives a power cut. Calling it per write gives you ~200 writes/s on a laptop; batching writes and syncing once gives you ~50,000/s at the cost of a small window. That trade-off is database engineering — make it explicit in a config.

Recovery: replay until the record breaks

A partially written final record is expected after a crash. Stopping at the first bad record — rather than erroring — is what makes the store crash-safe.

The read path

A bloom filter is 10 lines of hashing and removes ~99% of pointless disk reads. Add it in milestone 5 and measure the hit-rate improvement in perf stat.

Prove it correct

Then kill the process randomly (cargo-fuzz, or a loop of kill -9 in a shell script) and assert every acknowledged write is still there. That test is worth more than a thousand unit tests.

Stretch goals

  • Compaction with a size-tiered policy.
  • scan(range) using SSTable block indexes.
  • A block cache (LRU) in front of the tables.
  • CRC per block instead of per record.
  • A tiny RESP server so redis-cli can talk to it.

Demo checklist

  • 100k writes, kill -9, restart, zero data loss
  • memory stays flat at 10M keys
  • proptest green over 10,000 random operation sequences
  • a perf stat comparison of sequential vs random reads
